HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H&P) NOTE

History:
• 45-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset shortness of breath and sharp right-sided back pain that worsens with deep inspiration (pleuritic).  
• Symptoms began earlier today.  
• Associated findings: coughed up small amounts of blood on two occasions, subjective “slight fever,” awareness of heartbeat but pulse counted at home as regular, two-week history of fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance.  
• Denies recent long-haul travel, leg pain/swelling, or prior clots.  
• Non-smoker; works a desk job; lives alone in a flat; has a cat.

Past Medical History:
• Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).  
• No past clots, surgeries, or other chronic illnesses reported.

Allergies:
• No known drug or other allergies.

Medications:
• Methotrexate – dose/route/frequency not documented (took dose this morning).

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears clinically stable on video consultation.  
• Vital signs: Heart rate estimated 66-74 bpm, regular (radial pulse count). Temperature, BP, RR, SpO₂ not recorded.  
• Peripheral: Capillary refill brisk.  
• HEENT: Oropharynx normal on video; no cervical lymphadenopathy; patient reports no palpable neck glands.  
• Respiratory & Cardiovascular: No auscultation performed (tele-consult). No visible respiratory distress.  
• Abdomen/Extremities/Neuro: Not recorded.

Impression:
Likely community-acquired pneumonia / chest infection based on acute pleuritic pain, cough with haemoptysis, and subjective fever in an immunosuppressed patient.

DDx (consistent with transcript):
1. Community-acquired pneumonia – most probable.  
2. Pulmonary embolism – consider given triad (pleuritic pain, SOB, haemoptysis) and SLE-related clot risk.  
3. Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis or alveolar haemorrhage – less likely but possible.

Management Plan:
• Arrange same-day face-to-face GP review for:  
  – Full vital signs (BP, temp, RR, SpO₂)  
  – Chest auscultation and cardiovascular exam  
  – Consider chest X-ray and baseline bloods if abnormal findings or no improvement.  
• Hold off on prescribing antibiotics until in-person assessment; likely to start empiric antibiotic therapy if bacterial infection confirmed.  
• Provide support-team phone number for patient to book today’s clinic visit.  
• Educated patient that presentation more suggestive of infection than lung cancer; further investigations (e.g., chest X-ray) if symptoms persist.  
• Advised to seek urgent care (A&E) for worsening breathlessness, increasing haemoptysis, high fever, or chest pain.

Patient Summary:
45-year-old woman with SLE on methotrexate developed acute pleuritic back pain, dyspnoea, fever, and minor haemoptysis today. Tele-exam stable; most consistent with pneumonia. Same-day in-person review arranged for examination and potential antibiotics.

Key Takeaways:
• Attend clinic today for physical examination and possible antibiotic treatment.  
• Call support team immediately to book appointment.  
• Seek emergency care if symptoms worsen (severe SOB, profuse blood in sputum, high fever).

Next Steps:
• In-person assessment with vitals and lung exam.  
• Chest X-ray and labs if indicated.  
• Initiate antibiotics or further work-up (e.g., D-dimer/CTPA) based on examination findings.  
• Re-evaluate after treatment or within 48–72 h if no improvement.
